title: Install manual and automatic filters for an irrigation system

lessons.title: Why irrigation water needs filtering
lessons.html:
The need for filtration

Water from a dam, river, borehole or even a municipal pipe carries small bits of dirt. You often cannot see them. In an irrigation system these bits cause problems:

  • Drippers and small sprinkler nozzles get blocked.
  • Plants next to a blocked dripper get no water and die.
  • Sprinklers throw unevenly, so some areas are dry and some are wet.
  • Valves leak because dirt stops them closing.
  • Pumps and meters wear out faster.

Filters catch the dirt before it gets into the pipes. Cleaning a filter is quick and cheap. Replacing blocked drippers is slow and expensive.

What is in the water

DirtWhere it comes from
Sand and siltBoreholes, rivers, broken pipes
Algae and slimeDams and open tanks in sunlight
Leaves, insects, snails, frog eggsDams, rivers, canals
Rust and scaleOld steel pipes, hard water
Plastic bits and glueNew pipe installation, if pipes were not flushed

How fine must the filter be?

The smaller the hole in the emitter, the finer the filter must be. Drip systems need finer filtering than pop-up sprinklers. The filter fineness is given in mesh or micron. Always use the grade the dripper or sprinkler maker asks for. Your supervisor or the design will tell you.

A filter that is too coarse lets dirt through. A filter that is much too fine blocks very fast and causes high pressure loss.

Remember

Always flush new pipes before you fit the emitters, so building dirt does not go straight into the system.

lessons.title: Filter elements and manual versus automatic filters
lessons.html:
The filter element

The element is the part inside the filter that catches the dirt.

ElementWhat it looks likeGood for
Screen (mesh)A tube of fine steel or plastic meshSand and hard bits; municipal and borehole water
DiscA stack of thin plastic rings with tiny grooves, pressed togetherSand and soft dirt like algae; easy to clean
Sand or mediaA tank filled with special filter sandLots of algae and organic dirt, such as dam water
Sand separator (hydrocyclone)A cone that spins the waterHeavy sand from boreholes and rivers

Disc and screen elements often have colour codes to show their fineness. Never put in an element of a different grade without asking.

Manual filters

A manual filter must be opened and cleaned by hand.

  • Cheap and simple.
  • But someone must remember to clean it. If it blocks, pressure drops and plants suffer.
  • Cleaning stops the irrigation while the filter is open.
  • Dirty water can get past when the element is taken out, if it is not done carefully.

Automatic self-flushing filters

An automatic filter cleans itself. When it gets dirty, the pressure difference across it rises. A control unit then opens a flush valve and washes the dirt out to a drain. Some flush on a timer.

  • No one needs to be there.
  • The system keeps working while it flushes, especially with banks of several filters.
  • Good for dirty water and large systems like sportsfields and farms.
  • Costs more and needs enough water pressure to flush.

Cleaning a manual filter

  1. Turn off the water and release the pressure.
  2. Open the housing and take out the element.
  3. Wash it with clean water and a soft brush. Do not tear the mesh.
  4. Check the seals, put it back, close and turn on slowly.

lessons.title: Where to install filters and which valves to include
lessons.html:
Positions for filters

The filter must be placed where it protects the system and is easy to reach.

  • At the pump station: after the pump, and after the fertiliser injection point, so any undissolved fertiliser is also caught. This is the main filter.
  • Before a pump: only a coarse suction strainer or foot valve strainer; a fine filter on the suction side starves the pump.
  • At the start of each drip zone: a smaller safety filter after the zone valve, as a second line of protection.
  • On a municipal connection: after the meter and backflow preventer, before the zone valves.
  • Hydrocyclone: before the main filter, to take out heavy sand first.

Put the filter where it is protected from damage, has a firm base and has space to open it and clean it. The flush water must drain away from the pump house and electric panel.

Valves to include

ValveWhy
Isolating valve before and after the filterTo shut off the water for cleaning without draining pipes
Bypass with a valve (optional)To keep water flowing in an emergency; keep it closed in normal use
Pressure gauges or test points before and afterTo see the pressure difference and know when to clean
Air release valveTo let trapped air out
Flush or drain valveTo wash out dirt
Non-return valveWhere water must not flow back through the filter

Installing

  1. Check the flow arrow on the filter body and fit it the right way round.
  2. Use the correct fittings and support the filter so the pipe does not carry its weight.
  3. Flush the pipe before connecting.
  4. Turn on slowly and check for leaks.
  5. Write down the clean pressure difference.

Key points

  • Filters stop dirt blocking drippers, nozzles and valves.
  • Use the filter grade the emitter maker asks for.
  • Screen, disc, sand and hydrocyclone filters suit different dirt.
  • Automatic filters clean themselves; manual filters must be cleaned by hand.
  • Install the main filter after the pump and fertiliser injector, with isolating valves and gauges.
